אל
אל
So in the phrase יֶשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי it is in the
power of my hand, in my power, e. g.
Gen. 31, 29 יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי לַעֲשׂוֹת עִמָּכֶם רָעָה.
Prov. 3, 27. Mic. 2, 1; also negatively,
Deut. 28, 32 אֵין לְאֵל יָדֶךָ nothing is in
the power of thy hand, thou canst avail
nothing. Neh. 5, 5. The לְ here indi-
cates state or condition. Some, with a
very slight perception of the nature of
this phrase, understand אֵל of God, and
render: my hand is for God, i. e. instead
of God, comp. Job 12, 6. Hab. 1, 11; also
Virg. Æn. 10. 773 Dextra mihi Deus,
etc. Those passages are indeed paral-
lel among themselves; but have nothing
to do with this phrase. See in אֱלֹהַּ.
3. God, the Mighty One, the Almighty.
In order to illustrate how far the Hebrew
usage in respect to the names of God, as
אֵל, אֱלֹהִים, יְהֹוָה, יָהּ, is synonymous,
we note here the following in respect to
this word: a) In prose, when spoken of
God κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν, it never stands alone,
but always either with an attribute, as
אֵל חַי, אֵל קַנָּא, אֵל שַׁדַּי, אֵל עֶלְיוֹן; or with
another name of God, as אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Gen. 33, 20; הָאֵל אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ Gen. 46, 3;
אֵל אֱלֹהִים יְהֹוָה Josh. 22, 22. Ps. 50, 1,
where it may be rendered, God of gods,
Jehovah, comp. Dan. 11, 36 אֵל אֵלִים; or
lastly with the genitive of a place or
person of which God is called the God,
as אֵל בֵּית־אֵל Gen. 31, 13. b) Far more
frequently it is the poetic name for God,
and stands in poetry very often alone,
sometimes with the art. הָאֵל, Ps. 18, 31.
33. 48. 68, 21. Job 8, 3. c) It takes the
suff. of 1 pers. אֵלִי my God! Ps. 18, 3.
22, 2. 11. The other suffixes are never
found with it; and for thy God, his God,
etc. is always said אֱלֹהֶיךָ, אֱלֹהָיו. d) It
is also a general name for a divinity, and
is thus used of idols; either alone Is. 44,
10. 15; or with an epithet, as אֵל אַחֵר an-
other god Ex. 34, 14, אֵל זָר a strange
god Ps. 81, 10.
To God is said in Scripture to belong
whatever is excellent, distinguished,
superior in its kind; since the ancients
were accustomed to refer all excellence
directly to the deity as its immediate
author. Hence אַרְזֵי אֵל Ps. 80, 11 cedars
of God, i. e. the loftiest, most beautiful,
as if planted by Jehovah; comp. עֲצֵי
So הַרְרֵי אֵל mountains of God Ps. 36, 7.
Comp. ἅλς δῖα, δῖα Λακεδαίμων. See in
אֱלֹהִים no. 6.
Plur. אֵלִים 1. mighty ones, heroes;
see above in Sing. no. 1.
2. gods, in a wider sense, spoken of
Jehovah and also heathen gods, Ex. 15,
11, comp. 18, 11. Dan. 11, 36 אֵל אֵלִים
God of gods, i. e. the supreme God. Also
בְּנֵי אֵלִים Ps. 29, 1. 89, 7, sons of the gods,
by an idiom of Heb. and Syriac syntax,
poet. for sons of God, i. e. angels.
Note. Following the example of most
etymologists, we have above referred אֵל
to the root אוּל; but to speak more accu-
rately, אֵל would seem rather to be a
primitive word, yet adapted in a certain
measure to an etymology from אוּל, so
that to the mind of the Hebrew it always
presented the idea of strength and power.
However this may be, we may note in
respect to Semitic usage: a) That from
the word אֵל (Arab. إِيلٌ, إِلٌ, and إِلٌّ)
as from a root or stem, are formed several
other derivative words, e. g. אָלָה to invoke
God, espec. in an oath; אָלַּהּ, أَلَّهَ, to wor-
ship God; also אֱלוֹהַּ, אֱלָהּ, إِلَاهٌ, God;
comp. ܐܰܒܳܗ to be a father, ܐܰܒܳܗ̈ܳܬܳܐ fathers,
from ܐܰܒ. b) That in Hebrew, besides
אֵל, which follows the analogy of verbs
ע״ו, there are two other forms follow-
ing the analogy of verbs ל״ה, viz.
אֵל, אֱלִי, which are usual in pr. names,
comp. אֶלְיָקִים, אֶלְיָשִׁיב, אֱלִימֶלֶךְ, etc.—
Among the Phenicians, ἬΛ, Ἴλος, was
used κατ᾿ ἐξοχήν of Saturn; see Monum.
Phœnic. p. 406.
II. אֵל pron. plur. i. q. אֵלֶּה these, Lat.
hi, hæ, hæc, found only in the Pentateuch
and in 1 Chr. 20, 8. Kindred is the form
of the art. הַל, Arab. ٱلْ.
III. אֵל, only in constr. אֶל, almost al-
ways with Makkeph, (without Makk.
2 Sam. 8, 7. 1 K. 7, 34,) rarely and poet.
in Plur. constr. אֱלֵי Job 3, 22. 5, 26.
15, 22. 29, 19, (comp. Arab. إِلَى,) plur. c.
suff. אֵלַי, אֵלֶיךָ, אֵלָיו, אֵלֵינוּ, אֲלֵיכֶם,
אֲלֵיהֶם and אֲלֵהֶם, once אֱלֵיהֶם Ez. 31. 14,
poet. אֱלֵימוֹ Ps. 2, 5; pr. a subst. implying
motion and direction to or towards a

line_status.note: Under the yod of יֶשׁ the print shows three dots (segol), not two (tsere); Reading A is correct. Rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.
The last word is printed רָעָה with a final he (feminine form, as in the MT of Gen. 31:29), not רָע; and the yod of יֵשׁ carries tsere (two dots), not segol. Reading B matches on both points.

Only three consonants are printed (א ל ה) with holam directly over the lamed — no vav — and the he carries a mapiq dot inside plus patah beneath, matching Reading B's defective אֱלֹהַּ rather than A's plene אֱלוֹהַ.

The only difference is the elision mark after κατ: the print shows a curved Greek apostrophe (koronis-shaped, matching the following Greek), not a straight ASCII quote, so the Greek elision mark U+1FBD of Reading B is correct. All other letters, breathings and accents (ἐξοχήν) are identical and match the print.

In both occurrences the holem dot is printed above the he (to the right of the vav) and the qamets sits under the vav, i.e. יְהֹוָה; Reading A swaps the two points (qamets under he, holem over vav), which is not what is printed.

All three Arabic words carry hamza-below + kasra on the alif and dammatan on the lam; only the third also has shadda (taller two-level stack). A wrongly gives the second word shadda and the third hamza-above/fatha; B omits the dammatan and adds sukun.

Space before the semicolon is printed (B right). Under the aleph the mark has a vertical tail — qamets, not patach (A right). The lamed shows a dagesh dot in its stem, and the Arabic lam carries a shadda with fatha above it (B right), so the line is a mix of both readings.

Third item is Arabic إِلَاهٌ (hamza-below alif with kasra, lam-alif, ha bearing damma-tanwin), not Syriac as in B; but the first Hebrew form is printed with mappiq (הַּ) as B has it, which A omits, and A lacks the tanwin.

The first Syriac word ends in ܗ (he, matching the ܐܒ- of the following ܐܒܗ̈ܬܐ and the root ܐܒ on the next line), not in a second alaph as Reading A has; the two angular marks above are the pthaha and zqapha vowel points. The second word is identical in both readings and matches the print.

The Hebrew item is ע״ו (verbs ʿayin-vav): a full final vav is printed after the ayin with the gershayim mark above, exactly parallel to ל״ה on the next line. Reading B drops the vav and misreads the gershayim as a holem.

The only mark above the Hebrew is the double-stroke gershayim sitting between lamed and he (the standard abbreviation for lamed-he verbs); no holem dot is printed on the lamed, so Reading B's לֹ is spurious.
Under the aleph of the first word the print shows two horizontal dots (tsere, אֵל), not the three-dot hataf segol that appears under the aleph of the second word אֱלִי; Reading B's אֱל is wrong.

Printed left-to-right order after "comp." is אֶלְיָקִים, then אֶלְיָשִׁיב, then אֱלִימֶלֶךְ (immediately before "etc.—"); Reading A reverses the list. Vowel points in B match the print (segol+sheva on the first two, hataf-segol on אֱלִימֶלֶךְ, shin dot present, final kaf with sheva).
Print shows smooth breathing + acute over both Η and Ι; A drops the acute on ΗΛ (Ἠ), B has the right marks but as spacing diacritic + bare capital rather than precomposed Ἤ/Ἴ.

The Arabic article is printed with alif-waṣla (ٱ, the flat ṣād-like mark above the alif) and sukūn on the lām, not hamza+fatḥa (A) or alif+fatḥa (B). The Hebrew הַל and the English match both readings.

The decisive point is the vowel under the aleph of the third form (before "Ez. 31. 14"): the print shows a three-dot hateph-segol (אֱ), not a two-dot tsere (אֵ) as in Reading B; this is exactly the anomalous form Gesenius is singling out with "once". The rest is identical in both readings and matches the print (first form plene with yod, second defective without yod).

Under the aleph of אלימו the print shows three dots in the ḥateph-segol arrangement (shewa plus segol), not the two horizontal dots of tsere; lamed carries tsere, then plene yod and mem with ḥolem-vav. Rest of the line identical in both readings.
